PDF Accessibility Tag Checker

Checks a PDF's internal structure against the requirements PDF/UA and Section 508 are actually built from: is it a tagged PDF (a structure tree a screen reader can follow), does it have a title and a declared language, do its images have alternate text, do form fields have an accessible name, and does every page have a real text layer rather than being an un-OCR'd scan. Runs entirely in your browser -- the file is never uploaded. Preparing for ADA Title II's April 2027/2028 deadlines? PDFs your site links are "web content" under that rule too.

1. Choose a PDF (nothing is uploaded)

Drag a PDF here, or

Waiting for a file.

Report

2. Or batch-scan a whole document library with the CLI

Node.js, no dependencies to install -- checks the exact same things as the browser page:

node cli/check.mjs ./document-library/ --json

Get check.mjs, engine.mjs, and pdf-parser.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever reads the files you point it at; nothing goes through this site. Point it at a folder to scan every .pdf in it (recursively), or list files directly. Exits non-zero if any file has a finding, so it works as a CI or scheduled-job gate.

Common questions

Does a clean report mean my PDF is PDF/UA or Section 508 compliant?

No. This checks a specific set of automatable structural signals -- tagging, title, language, an approximate image/alt-text count, form-field labels, and whether a page has a text layer at all. It cannot judge whether an alt-text string is accurate, whether the reading order is actually correct, or run a real assistive-technology test. Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific checks, not a compliance determination -- PDF/UA and Section 508 both require things this tool cannot verify from structure alone.

Is my PDF uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page reads the file you choose entirely inside your own tab, using the browser's native DecompressionStream API to read compressed PDF streams -- nothing is sent to this site or anywhere else. The CLI reads the file directly on your own machine. This matters for government and legal documents that may contain information you would rather not hand to a third-party server, which is what most other free online PDF accessibility checkers ask you to do.

Why does this check PDF tags instead of just running a visual accessibility scanner?

A PDF's accessibility to a screen reader depends on structure that isn't visible on the page at all: a tag tree describing reading order and roles, a declared language, and alternate text attached to images in the structure tree, not just present somewhere in the file. PDF/UA and Section 508 are both built around this "tagged PDF" requirement, so checking the structure directly is what actually answers the question, the same way an HTML accessibility checker reads the DOM rather than a screenshot.

What does the "approximate" alt-text count actually mean?

This tool counts image objects in the document and, separately, structure-tree elements that carry non-empty alt text, and compares the two totals. It does not walk the marked-content ID chain that maps one specific structure element to one specific image, so it cannot say for certain which image is missing alt text -- only whether the document-wide totals suggest some or all of them are. Zero alt-bearing elements against one or more images is reported as a clear finding; a partial count is reported as a notice to review by hand.

Why is there also a CLI, not just the browser page?

A government IT office or university disability-services team usually has a document library, not one PDF -- an accessibility pass means checking hundreds of them. The CLI takes a folder and reports every PDF in it in one run, which is the shape you actually want for a batch remediation project or a recurring CI/scheduled check on newly-published documents. It shares the exact same checking code as the browser page, so the two can never silently disagree.

Preparing web-page (not PDF) evidence for the same deadline? See the ADA Title II deadline lookup and WCAG evidence report. Buying software rather than publishing your own PDFs? See the VPAT/ACR generator for a vendor's own accessibility conformance report.

It is not a full PDF/UA or Section 508 conformance audit, cannot judge whether alt text is accurate or reading order is correct, and does not replace a manual or assistive-technology review.

vs-uploading-to-an-online-checker.html.text:
← Back to the PDF Accessibility Tag Checker

PDF/UA checker: in-browser vs. uploading to an online checker

Several free PDF/UA and Section 508 checkers already exist online -- PDFix, PDF Audit, freepdfchecker.com, and axesCheck among them -- and there is a well-known free desktop tool, PAC. The question worth asking before choosing one is not which finds the most issues; the structural checks in this class of tool are largely the same checks. It is what happens to the file you hand it, and whether you can check more than one at a time.

What actually differs

Where the file goes The surveyed free online checkers (PDFix, PDF Audit, freepdfchecker.com, axesCheck) read your PDF by first uploading it to their server. This checker's browser page reads the file with the browser's own File and DecompressionStream APIs, entirely in your tab -- nothing is sent anywhere. For a government form, a permit, meeting minutes, or an HR document, that is often the reason to be reluctant to hand a file to an unfamiliar site in the first place.
One file or a folder PAC, the classic free desktop tool, checks one file at a time. None of the surveyed free online checkers offer a batch or folder mode either. This tool's CLI, cli/check.mjs, walks a whole folder recursively (node cli/check.mjs ./document-library/ --json) and exits non-zero if any file has a finding -- so a document library of hundreds of PDFs is one command, and the same command can gate a CI job on newly published documents.
What it costs to run again Re-checking a PDF after a fix with an online checker means uploading it again. Re-checking here means dropping the file again or re-running the CLI -- no account, no queue, no per-file limit.

What does not differ

The structural checks themselves are the ordinary PDF/UA and Section 508 building blocks any tool in this class looks at: a tagged structure tree, a document title, a declared language, image alt text, an extractable text layer instead of an un-OCR'd scan, and accessible names on form fields. None of that is unique to this tool, and none of it is a substitute for a manual or assistive-technology review -- see the checker's own disclaimer on index.html for exactly what a clean report does and does not mean.

Common questions

Do free online PDF accessibility checkers upload my file to a server?

The ones surveyed here do -- PDFix, PDF Audit, freepdfchecker.com, and axesCheck all ask you to choose or drop a file that is then sent to their server to be scanned. This checker reads the file with the browser's own File and DecompressionStream APIs entirely in your tab, so a government form, a permit, or an HR document never has to leave your machine to be checked.

Can I check a whole folder of PDFs at once instead of one at a time?

Yes, with the CLI: node cli/check.mjs ./document-library/ --json walks a folder recursively and exits non-zero if any file has a finding, so it can gate a CI job or a scheduled task. The classic free desktop tool, PAC, checks one file at a time with no batch mode, and none of the surveyed free online checkers offer a batch or folder option either.

Does a clean report mean the PDF is fully PDF/UA or Section 508 compliant?

No. This is evidence, not a determination -- specific, automatable structural checks (tagging, title, language, alt-text coverage, text layer, form labels), not a full PDF/UA or Section 508 conformance audit and not a substitute for a manual or assistive-technology review. A clean report means these checks found nothing, not that the document is compliant.

What does this check that a visual read-through of the PDF would not catch?

It reads the file's internal structure rather than how it renders: whether the document catalog declares /MarkInfo /Marked true and a /StructTreeRoot, a non-empty /Title and a well-formed /Lang tag, whether image elements in the structure tree carry non-empty /Alt text, whether a page has an extractable text layer or is likely an un-OCR'd scan, and whether interactive form fields have an accessible name. None of that is visible just by looking at the rendered page.

← Back to the checker to drop in your own PDF, or use the CLI to batch-scan a folder.

why-does-my-pdf-fail-when-it-looks-fine..text:
← Back to the PDF Accessibility Tag Checker

Why does a PDF that looks fine fail this accessibility check?

Because PDF/UA and Section 508's tagging requirement is about a structure tree stored inside the file, not about how the page renders. A PDF viewer paints a page from raw drawing instructions -- position this text run here, draw this image there -- and can produce a perfectly readable page with no structure tree at all. A screen reader does not see the rendered page; it reads the tag tree, and if that tree is missing, incomplete, or never marked current, there is nothing for it to read regardless of how the page looks to a sighted reviewer.

This gap is why a document can pass every eyeball review a team gives it and still fail a structural check outright: the two are looking at different things. Below is what each of this tool's six findings actually means and, where there is one, the ordinary fix.

Not a tagged PDF

The document catalog has no /StructTreeRoot at all, or has one but never declares /MarkInfo /Marked true -- so a reader cannot trust that whatever tree exists is complete or current. This is by far the most common finding, because tagging is opt-in at export time in most authoring tools: a Word document saved as PDF without "Best for electronic distribution and accessibility" checked, or a design tool's PDF export run without its accessibility pass, both produce a visually normal document with nothing structural underneath. The fix happens upstream, at export -- in Word, Export > Options > "Document structure tags for accessibility"; in Acrobat Pro, the Accessibility > "Autotag Document" or "Make Accessible" wizard adds a tree to a PDF that already exists.

No document title or no declared language

Both are single dictionary entries -- /Title in the Document Information dictionary, /Lang in the document catalog -- and both are invisible in a normal read-through because neither one renders on the page. Without a title, a screen reader announces the file name instead (scan0047.pdf is not useful to anyone); without a declared language, assistive technology has no signal for which pronunciation rules to load, even in a document written entirely in one language throughout.

How can a document have no text layer if I can read the text on the page?

The page you see is usually a scanned image of a printed document, not real text -- common for signed forms, older records, and anything run through a copier before being saved as a PDF. Visually the words are sharp and legible; structurally the page is one large picture with no text-show operator anywhere in its content stream, so nothing can be selected, searched, copied, or read aloud. The fix is OCR: running the page through optical character recognition to add a real, invisible text layer underneath the image.

My PDF has alt text on some images -- why is that still flagged?

A partial-alt-text finding is document-wide: it counts every image in the file against every non-empty /Alt string found anywhere in the structure tree, because matching a specific alt-text entry to the exact image it labels needs the marked-content ID chain this tool does not walk. If the counts are close, most images are likely labelled and a manual pass can confirm which ones are not; if the alt-text count is far below the image count, most images still have nothing, even though the file clearly has alt text on some of them.

Unlabeled form fields

An interactive form field can look perfectly labelled on the page -- a text box sitting right next to the words "Last name" -- while carrying no /TU (alternate field name) on itself or any ancestor field. The visible label and the field are two separate objects with no structural connection between them; a sighted user's eye makes the association a screen reader cannot. The fix is setting each field's tooltip/alternate name in the PDF form editor so the connection exists in the file, not just on the page.

Check your own document

Drop a PDF into the checker to see exactly which of these findings apply to it, with the specific evidence behind each one, or scan a whole folder at once with the CLI: 

node cli/check.mjs ./document-library/ --json

Neither the browser page nor the CLI uploads the file anywhere -- see the disclaimer below.
